texts.title: The Harbour Clock Comes Back
texts.text:
## Why the clock stopped
The old clock above the harbour kept good time for many decades. Salt air rusted its gears until one of them jammed. Fishing crews noticed first, because they set their days by its bell. The tower is painted white and blue.

## Who will do the work
Odile Marsh learned her trade in a small shop on the quay. A retired clockmaker, Odile Marsh, will lead the repair. Two apprentices from the school will help her.

## What it will cost
Parts and paint come to a modest sum. Most of the money will come from donations left in a glass jar at the bakery. The jar was first put on the counter last spring.

## When it will finish
The work starts in the first week of winter. Rain may cause delays, so the date is a hope and not a promise. The bell should ring again by the first day of spring.

## How to help
Volunteers are welcome on Saturdays to sand and paint the tower. Please bring gloves and an old shirt. Tea is served from a small cart.

texts.title: A New Bus Route for Marrow Hill
texts.text:
## Why a new route
Many families on Marrow Hill cannot easily reach the market. The old bus stopped at the bottom of the slope. Carrying shopping uphill was hard for everyone.

## The route
Bus 12 will run in a loop from the market, up the hill and back. It will pass the school, the library and the park. The new buses are painted green.

## The timetable
A bus will leave every hour, starting at seven in the morning. Extra buses will run when school ends. The last bus of the day leaves at seven in the evening.

## Tickets
Tickets can be bought from the driver. A ticket will cost the same as on every other bus in town. Children under five ride for free.

## Start date
The new route begins on the first Monday of June. Printed maps will be at the library and the market. The mayor will ride the first bus.

texts.title: The Lantern Festival of Thistlefen
texts.text:
## The beginning
The festival began long ago to light the darkest night of winter. Farmers carried lamps down to the river. Nobody knows who first suggested it. It has been held every year since, even in heavy rain.

## The lanterns
Each lantern is made of paper and a thin wooden frame. Children paint them during the week before the festival. Many of the lanterns show fish or owls.

## The parade
Drummers lead the way. The parade walks from the church to the old stone bridge. The walk takes about half an hour.

## The river
At the bridge, small lanterns are set afloat on the river. People make a wish as they let go. A few lanterns always get stuck in the reeds.

## Food and warmth
The square fills with the smell of cooking. Volunteers serve hot pumpkin soup in the square. The festival ends when the last lantern floats out of sight. Hot cider is sold at the stalls by the bridge.

texts.title: The Tarnwick Library Annex Opens
texts.text:
## What is new
The annex adds a children's room and a quiet study hall. It is built of pale brick. The study hall has twenty desks and good lighting. The reading chairs were made by a local carpenter.

## Opening day
The annex opens on Saturday the third of May. The mayor will cut a ribbon at ten o'clock. Everyone is welcome to come along. Cake and lemonade will be served in the garden after the ceremony. Local school choirs will sing two songs.

## Opening hours
Weekend hours are shorter. On weekdays it will stay open until nine in the evening. The old building will keep its usual hours.

## Joining
Bring a letter that shows your address. Anyone in town can join with a free library card. Cards are printed on the spot.

## Events
Story time for small children runs every Thursday morning. Parents can stay and read along. A chess club meets in the study hall.

texts.title: Why the Dunmarrow Bakery Changed Its Hours
texts.text:
## The change
The shop still closes at the usual time. The bakery now opens one hour earlier, at six. Signs in the window explain the change. Early customers get a free roll on the first morning.

## The reason
The owner heard the same request again and again. Some customers had been buying bread from the supermarket instead. Many people on their way to early shifts wanted fresh bread. Two cafes nearby also open at six.

## The first loaves
The first loaves out of the oven are rye and sourdough. Soft rolls come a little later. The rye flour comes from a mill upriver.

## The new helper
A new apprentice named Tomas helps with the early baking. He is learning how to shape rolls. He cycles in from the next village.

## Sundays
Orders for weddings are taken on Mondays. The bakery stays closed on Sundays so the family can rest. The sign on the door says so in large letters.

texts.title: The Reef Garden Project at Perrin Cove
texts.text:
## The idea
Divers plan to grow small pieces of coral on frames. The frames sit in shallow, sunny water. The project is a partnership between divers and the town council. Growth is slow, so the project will take years.

## The frames
Each frame is built from rope. A mesh of fibre holds the coral fragments in place. The first six frames were built by volunteers.

## The helpers
Students from the cove school will check the frames every month. Each class adopts one frame. Parents are invited to the monthly dive reports. They keep a notebook of what they see.

## The fish
Small fish need places to hide from big ones. The frames act as a nursery where young fish shelter. Crabs and shrimp move in as well.

## How to visit
Boats leave from the harbour wall. Visitors can see the garden from a glass-bottom boat. The trip takes about forty minutes. Bring a hat and sunscreen for the trip.

texts.title: How Bees Make Honey
texts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, "honey"; USDA National Agricultural Library bee pages
texts.text:
## Collecting nectar
Worker bees fly out and collect nectar from flowers. They sip it up through a long tongue called a proboscis. Bees also carry pollen on their back legs.

## The honey stomach
The bee stores the nectar in a special honey stomach, which is separate from its food stomach. Back at the hive it passes the nectar to a house bee.

## Turning nectar into honey
House bees pass the nectar from mouth to mouth. They add enzymes that change the sugars in the nectar. The enzymes come from glands in the bee's body.

## Drying it
The nectar thickens as it dries. Bees fan it with their wings to drive off the water. The hive stays warm to help the water leave.

## Storing the honey
The finished honey is sealed in wax cells to keep it fresh. The bees make the wax themselves. The cells of a honeycomb have six sides.

texts.title: How a Rainbow Forms
texts.source: NOAA National Weather Service rainbow pages; Encyclopaedia Britannica, "rainbow"
texts.text:
## Sunlight and rain
A rainbow needs sunlight and raindrops at the same time. The sun must be behind you and the rain in front of you. It often appears just after a shower.

## Entering the drop
Sunlight looks white but is made of many colours. Blue and violet light bends more than red light does. Light bends as it enters a raindrop.

## Inside the drop
The light reflects off the back of the drop. Some of the light escapes straight through instead. The path inside the drop is a short curve.

## Leaving the drop
Each colour leaves at a slightly different angle. As it leaves, the light bends again and spreads out into colours.

## What you see
Red is on the outside of the main rainbow and violet is on the inside. A second, fainter rainbow sometimes appears above it, with the colours in reverse. Many rainbows are only partly visible.

texts.title: Why the Sea Has Tides
texts.source: NOAA National Ocean Service, "Tides and Water Levels"
texts.text:
## The Moon's pull
The Moon's gravity pulls on the oceans and causes tides. The Sun also pulls on them, but less strongly. Tides are higher or lower depending on the shape of the coast.

## Two bulges
Water bulges toward the Moon and also on the far side of Earth. Each bulge makes a high tide. The bulges are small in the open ocean and larger near some coasts.

## Two high tides
Earth turns beneath the bulges. Most coasts have two high tides and two low tides each day. A few places have only one.

## Spring tides
The biggest tides happen at new Moon and full Moon, when the Sun and Moon line up. They are called spring tides, but the name has nothing to do with the season.

## Neap tides
The smallest tides happen at the quarter Moons. Then the Sun and Moon pull at right angles to each other. Harbours print tide tables for each month.

texts.title: How Paper Is Made
texts.text:
## Fibres
Recycled paper uses old paper instead of new wood. Rags and cotton were used before wood became common. Most paper is made from the fibres of wood.

## Making pulp
Logs are chipped and cooked or ground into a wet pulp. Water is added until the mixture is mostly water. A pulp mill needs a steady supply of fresh water. Pulp may be bleached to make the paper whiter.

## Forming sheets
The thin pulp is spread over a moving screen so the water drains away. The fibres tangle together as they settle. The wet web of fibres is only a thin film at first.

## Pressing and drying
Rollers press the sheet and heated cylinders dry it. The sheet loses most of its water in this stage. The largest paper machines are as long as a street.

## Finishing
The paper is wound onto a huge reel and cut to size. Some papers get a coating for a glossy look.

texts.title: How Glass Is Made
texts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, "glass"; Corning Museum of Glass
texts.text:
## Ingredients
Glass is mostly made from sand. Soda ash and limestone are added to the mix. The ingredients are weighed carefully before mixing.

## Melting
The mixture has to be extremely hot. Workers must wear protective clothing near the furnace. It is melted in a furnace until it flows like thick syrup. Colour comes from tiny amounts of added metals.

## Shaping
Hot glass can be blown, pressed or poured flat. Window glass is often floated on a bath of melted tin. Skilled glassblowers shape small objects by hand. Bottles are shaped in metal moulds.

## Slow cooling
Cooling too fast leaves stress inside that can make it crack. Large pieces need longer to cool than small ones. Glass is cooled slowly in an oven, a step called annealing.

## Recycling
Broken glass, called cullet, can be melted again. Using cullet saves energy in the furnace. Glass can be recycled many times. Clear, green and brown glass are usually sorted first.

texts.title: The Lens in a Lighthouse
texts.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Fresnel lens"; United States Lighthouse Society
texts.text:
## The problem
A bare lamp lets most of its light spread out and fade. Sailors needed a light that could be seen far away. Early lighthouses burned wood or coal on open fires.

## A new lens
In the 1820s a French engineer, Augustin-Jean Fresnel, perfected a new kind of lens. It was built from rings of glass instead of one thick block. Fresnel was trained as an engineer in France.

## Rings of prisms
Glass prisms around the lamp bend its light into a narrow beam. The design uses much less glass than a solid lens would. It was first used at the Cordouan lighthouse in France in 1823.

## Turning
Each lighthouse has its own pattern of flashes. Turning the lens makes the beam sweep round and appear as a flash.

## Today
Many old lenses are now kept in museums. Many lighthouses now use modern lamps. Some lenses stand taller than a person.
